selected.name: Identifies and diagnoses the asker's specific error or confusion
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer pinpoints exactly where the asker's reasoning went wrong and explains the fix. Score 0 if it provides a correct solution without diagnosing what the asker was missing.
selected.rationale: R32 identifies the exact missing factor (365^23-2) and the uncounted scenarios, and R30 diagnoses the real vs. complex cube root confusion—both dense-high. R13 gives a correct recurrence solution without engaging the asker's specific confusion—dense-low.
member_names: Diagnosis of the misconception behind the question
Identifies and diagnoses the asker's specific error or confusion
Precise diagnosis of the asker's specific error or confusion

selected.name: Delivers a resolution rather than commentary about the question
selected.instruction: Score whether the answer actually resolves what was asked. 10 = the answer produces the thing the question asked for — the value, the proof, the construction, the definition, the decision — and hands it over. 5 = the answer supplies a partial resolution plus substantial commentary. 0 = the answer principally comments on, reframes, qualifies, or deflates the question rather than answering it: caveats about why the question is less interesting than it looks, disclaimers that this is not an answer, or discussion of what a cited author must have meant.
selected.rationale: R34 states outright 'This is not an answer to the question but a complement to the Robert Israel's answer' (dense 0.027 / card 0.959); R55 argues the asked-about phenomenon has 'less than meets the eye' and concludes 'the importance of parallel arrows in commutative squares? In general...none' (0.076 / 0.838); R25 supplies an important caveat about non-uniqueness rather than the requested construction (0.096 / 0.801); R08 spends its first half adjudicating what Dr. Stewart meant in a 1996 book (0.104 / 0.848). Contrast R23, which drives to '$(-\infty,-7]\cup[-5,+\infty)$. Done!' (0.903 / 0.086) and R21, which kills the claim with a three-line counterexample (0.740 / 0.032). A criterion bank rewards nuance and caveating; a resolution is what a single asker was after.
member_names: Delivers a resolution rather than commentary about the question
Reaches a clean terminus with no unresolved residue

selected.name: Edge-case coverage
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer explicitly identifies relevant domains, exceptional cases, and boundary behavior; score 0 when it silently assumes the generic case or mishandles a case that changes the result.
selected.rationale: R23 carefully handles zero-ring exceptions and R45 distinguishes competing cube-root interpretations; R10 and R24 leave important structural qualifications unclear.
member_names: Explicit treatment of edge cases or exceptions

selected.name: Self-contained exposition
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer includes the definitions, facts, and derivations needed to follow it without outside material; score 0 when essential reasoning is outsourced to links or unexplained references.
selected.rationale: R12 invokes an external integral identity without deriving it, and R44 supplies several external references while using specialized formulas; these contrast with more internally developed answers.
member_names: Self-contained without requiring other answers or links

selected.name: Proportionality of method
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the amount of detail and mathematical machinery is proportionate to the task while preserving the essential logic; score 0 when the answer is bloated or so compressed that key reasoning disappears.
selected.rationale: R05 and R46 are compact yet usable, while R33 and R50 contain extensive technical development that can obscure the immediate question.

selected.name: Teaches a transferable method, not just a single answer
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer imparts a reusable technique, principle, or way of thinking that applies beyond the specific problem. Score 0 if the answer solves only this one instance with no generalizable takeaway.
selected.rationale: R35 teaches base-b division as a general principle. R34 teaches recognizing Schröder-Bernstein structure. R30 teaches a grid-based divisor-counting method. All are dense_high. The scorecard may focus on correctness of the specific result and miss pedagogical transfer value.
member_names: Teaches a transferable method, not just a single answer

selected.name: Audience-level accessibility
selected.instruction: Score 10 when vocabulary and machinery match the apparent level of the question and advanced ideas are explained; score 0 when a simple issue is buried under unexplained high-level machinery or the exposition is needlessly patronizing.
selected.rationale: R15 and R44 explain elementary methods plainly, whereas R34 and R38 introduce advanced machinery disproportionate to what the question appears to require.
member_names: Calibration to the asker's apparent mathematical level
Sophistication level matched to the question

selected.name: Direct verdict on the asker's own posted work
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer explicitly evaluates the specific reasoning, computation, or attempt the asker posted in their question -- confirming it is correct, or pinpointing exactly where and why it goes wrong (e.g. naming a specific step, line, or substitution the asker used). Score 0 if the answer never engages with anything the asker specifically wrote or tried, and instead addresses only the abstract problem.
selected.rationale: Rows R11 ('So your work is correct'), R31 ('your method isn't counting scenarios like...'), R33 ('Your DFA looks good to me'), and R47 ('There may be some little mistakes in your computation') all directly assess the asker's own attempt and sit in dense_high_card_low; this kind of direct engagement may be exactly what the dense model perceives and the scorecard undervalues.
member_names: Direct verdict on the asker's own displayed work
Direct verdict on the asker's own posted work
Explicit verdict on the asker's own posted work

selected.name: Continuity with asker’s approach
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer explicitly adopts and advances the asker’s notation or proposed method; score 0 when it ignores that setup without need.
selected.rationale: R03 begins from the asker’s second technique, R46 evaluates the asker’s DFA and offers compatible next steps, and R57 works directly from the asker’s computation.
member_names: Direct engagement with the asker's own attempt
Engages with the asker's own attempt or framing

selected.name: Notation and logical discipline
selected.instruction: Score 10 when symbols, types, indices, quantifiers, and implication directions remain consistently defined; score 0 when notation or typing errors make the reasoning ambiguous or invalid.
selected.rationale: R60 carefully tracks the group action and stabilizer, while R10 and R48 exhibit ambiguity in the objects or logical steps being manipulated.

selected.name: Scope precision: answers exactly what is asked
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer addresses precisely the question asked—no more, no less—and stays tightly on topic. Score 0 if the answer wanders into extended philosophical discussion, addresses a different question, or vastly over-elaborates beyond what was asked.
selected.rationale: R15 gives a long philosophical discussion concluding 'none' about parallel arrows. R25 digresses into lexicographic ordering and Banach-Tarski. R31 is an ambitious write-up of a blog-post plan. All are dense_low. Askers accept answers that solve their problem, not encyclopedic essays.
member_names: Scope precision: answers exactly what is asked

selected.name: Proportional conciseness to question difficulty
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer's length, depth, and formality are well-matched to the difficulty of the question—brief for simple questions, fuller for complex ones. Score 0 if the answer is dramatically over-elaborated (treats a simple question like a research seminar) or under-elaborated (one-liner for a deep question).
selected.rationale: R10 answers a basic summation question in two lines and R36 gives a one-line counterexample; both are dense-high. R15 and R41 deliver near-lecture-length treatments that may overwhelm an asker who needs something shorter, and both are dense-low.
member_names: Length proportionate to the difficulty of the question

selected.name: Confidence without hedging or self-deprecation
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the answer is presented as a definitive, assured response to the question. Score 0 if the answer hedges with phrases like 'this might work,' 'I think,' or explicitly disclaims itself as not really an answer.
selected.rationale: R23 begins 'This is not an answer to the question' and R47 says 'the following might work'—both dense_low. Askers are less likely to accept answers whose authors signal uncertainty about their own contributions. The scorecard may not penalize this self-undermining.
member_names: Confident framing without hedging or disclaimers

selected.name: Complete proof coverage
selected.instruction: Score 10 when every central inference needed for the claimed result is justified, with 0 for a substantial unsupported leap or merely asserted conclusion.
selected.rationale: R17 connects the group action, differential, stabilizer, and embedding arguments, while R35 explains the conflicting cube-root manipulations step by step.

selected.name: Why-the-method explanation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the answer explains the underlying reason a method works in intuitive terms, and 0 when it is only a formula dump or sequence of unexplained operations.
selected.rationale: R27 explains equal-sized fibers of a mapping, R49 uses the puzzle-tile analogy for families of squares, and R37 explains why the notation records group structure.

selected.name: Markup density
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the answer uses dense display mathematics, custom macros, colored notation, boxed arrays, diagrams, headings, or other elaborate markup; do not judge whether the feature is good.
selected.rationale: R11 uses extensive color and alignment, R48 uses a Fitch-style custom macro, and R55 uses boxed grids. Such formatting fingerprints can reflect author habits and site fluency independently of mathematical quality.
selected.upstream_parent: author's practice in the site's markup format

Site-veteran markup habits: macro preambles, tags, spoilers

selected.name: Visible revision markers
selected.instruction: From 0 to 10, how many visible signs of post-hoc revision appear (e.g., 'EDIT', 'Edit:', 'after a long calculation', 'I just read your last post')? Judge extent only; do not judge whether editing is good or bad.
selected.rationale: Revision markers (R08, R44, R50) reflect submission dynamics that may affect model perception without relating to acceptance.
member_names: Post-hoc revision layering: EDIT blocks and addenda
Visible revision scars and appended amendment blocks
upstream_parent_all_members: post-hoc editing under comment pressure, and the amount of elapsed dwell time the author spent on the post after publishing

selected.name: External-resource citation and tool appeals
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the answer routes authority outside itself: hyperlinks or URLs, named databases and their identifiers (OEIS sequence numbers), computer-algebra appeals ('confirmed by Wolfram Alpha', 'try using WolframAlpha'), numbered theorem citations to named textbooks ('theorem 12.29 of Rudin's Functional Analysis'), formal bibliography entries with journals and DOIs, named editions of books, pointers to lecture notes, and 'see this link / this post'. 0 = wholly self-contained with no outward pointer; 10 = the substance is largely a set of pointers plus a formal reference list. Score the extent of outward pointing only. Do NOT judge whether the citations are authoritative, relevant, or well formatted.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. R15 is essentially a pointer to OEIS A038534 plus 'In this post there are references to formulas'; R53 appends three journal references with DOIs; R24 says 'This result is confirmed by Wolfram Alpha'; R36 advises 'For future, try using WolframAlpha for basic integrals'; R41 cites 'theorem 12.29 of Rudin's Functional Analysis'; R11 points at a colleague's unlinked course notes; R27 cites 'Dr. Stewart's 1996 edition of from here to infinity' and links 'lexicographic ordering is not a well ordering'. Citation habit tracks who the author is and what they have at hand rather than whether the answer met the asker's need; tagged mixed because a well-sourced pointer can itself be exactly what was wanted.
selected.upstream_parent: the answerer's access to and practice with external resources and literature (academic affiliation, tooling habits)
upstream_parent_all_members: author's academic standing and citation practice
author's practice of resourcefulness/scholarly formatting in the format
external assistance, tools, or institutional authority
external authority, assistance, and resource access
the answerer's access to and practice with external resources and literature (academic affiliation, tooling habits)

selected.name: Sheer bulk and display-mathematics density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of textual bulk and displayed-equation density, judged on volume alone: total length, number of separate display-math blocks and multi-line aligned environments, number of paragraph breaks, and presence of multi-stage derivation chains. 0 = one or two sentences with at most one displayed line; 10 = many screens of prose interleaved with a dozen or more display blocks. Count volume only, exactly as a word- and equation-counter would. Do NOT judge whether the length is warranted, whether the derivation is complete, or whether the answer is thorough.
selected.rationale: A pure size proxy, mechanically computable and therefore an easy shortcut for either model, and it varies by two orders of magnitude across the slice: R15 and R34 are single sentences, R38 is one line, whereas R44, R45, R52, R53 and R13 run to many display blocks and several thousand characters. It must be declared a nuisance so that neither model may bank on length; the asker's choice is not a word count.

selected.name: Prior-answer dependence
selected.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, rate how much the answer explicitly presupposes, supplements, corrects, or contrasts with earlier answers or comments; judge only visible wording, not whether this is good.
selected.rationale: R01 says it is posted separately from a first post, while R24 calls itself a complement to another answer and mentions an edit. Such wording fingerprints arrival after existing discussion and exposure to prior entries, a timing nuisance rather than a mathematical-quality criterion.
member_names: Deixis presupposing other answers already exist
Latecomer framing: presupposes other answers already exist
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream (how many answers had already been posted when this one arrived)
position in the entry stream (how many answers had already been posted when this one was written)
position in the entry stream (posted after other answers already existed)

selected.name: Author personality / conversational asides
selected.instruction: 0-10: rate how much informal, conversational, or humorous personal voice appears in the prose -- exclamations, jokes, emoticons, self-deprecating asides, a personal sign-off name, or direct colloquial address to the reader (e.g., 'Well, jolly gosh!', '^_^', 'Cheers! -Shahar', 'I hope this was helpful'). 0 = strictly impersonal, formal register throughout; 10 = pervasive informal/conversational personal voice. Do not judge whether the informality is charming or unprofessional -- score only how much of it is present.
selected.rationale: R10 ('Well, jolly gosh! ... Cheers! -Shahar') and R23 ('I hope this helps ^_^') are both dense_low_card_high, while R54 ('I hope this was helpful') is dense_high_card_low -- conversational voice appears on both sides of the split and is a personality tell, not an acceptance signal, so it must be discounted from both models symmetrically.
member_names: Emotive interjections, exclamation runs, sign-offs and signatures
upstream_parent_all_members: the author's register habit and inexperience in the format (a newer, more conversational contributor versus a terse practised one)

selected.name: Named participants, @handles and priority acknowledgements
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text names or tags other people in the thread or beyond it: @-handles, first names or usernames of other answerers and commenters, 'the OP' as a term of art, credit assignments ('as suggested by X', 'X got there first', 'expanding on a comment by X', 'with the help of a colleague'), and appeals to a named authority who reviewed the work. 0 = no person is named or tagged anywhere; 10 = several named participants are addressed or credited throughout. Score naming density only. Do NOT judge whether the credit is generous, deserved, or well placed.
selected.rationale: MODE 2. Social embedding is unobservable but leaves handles in the text. R34 opens '@supinf showed us a nice set of examples'; R12 refers to '@ReihardMeier's answer'; R23 addresses 'Asaf Shachar' twice; R09 credits 'a comment by Bill'; R10 opens 'Clive's answer is already a good one'; R57 'as suggested by Ted'; R24 'I acknowledge that Semiclassical got there first'; R28 'now validated by Prof. Shifrin'; R21 and R51 use 'OP' and name 'Robert Israel'. Being on first-name terms with the regulars is a standing/network property and is not a property of the answer's substance, so it is a declared nuisance rather than a mixed channel.
selected.upstream_parent: the answerer's social embedding in the site community (recognising and being recognised by other regulars)
member_names: Named or @-handled address of other site participants
Named-peer citation of other site users
upstream_parent_all_members: answerer's social embeddedness / standing and relationships within the site's community
social/conversation dynamics in the comment thread and the author's embeddedness in the site's regular community
the answerer's social embedding in the site community (recognising and being recognised by other regulars)

selected.name: Era-specific conventions
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the text exhibits platform-era conventions such as legacy notation, older markup habits, username references, edit conventions, or period-specific tool vocabulary; judge only visible vintage markers, not whether they are good.
selected.rationale: Different periods leave traces in notation, markup, terminology, and interaction conventions. Examples include legacy notation in R35, old-style macros in R54, and platform or tool references in R29 and R50; these are temporal nuisances rather than mathematical merit.

selected.name: Elementary-exercise versus research-register vocabulary
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the vocabulary and objects in the text belong to advanced or specialist mathematics rather than to routine early-coursework computation. Low scores: arithmetic, factors and divisors, basic differentiation and integration by substitution, elementary trigonometric identities, simple summation identities, textbook probability counting. High scores: named advanced machinery and specialist notation (Galois groups, cyclotomic fields, forcing and generic filters, Poincare-Hopf, Bell polynomials and Faa di Bruno, Jacobi theta functions, spectral theorem on Hilbert space, cardinal arithmetic with $2^{\mathfrak c}$). Score the register of the subject matter only. Do NOT judge difficulty as merit, and do NOT judge whether the answer handles its material well.
selected.rationale: Subject register is a proxy for the container the answer sits in -- how many rival answers arrived and how the thread was consumed -- rather than for the asker's selection. It splits the slice sharply: R21, R22, R35, R55 are elementary computations, while R13, R53, R56, R57, R52 are graduate/research-level; topic is not merit.
selected.upstream_parent: the kind of question the answer is attached to (a routine homework computation that one person wants closed versus a conceptual question that draws a crowd of answerers and spectators)
upstream_parent_all_members: kind of question and its likely specialist audience
the kind of question the answer is attached to (a routine homework computation that one person wants closed versus a conceptual question that draws a crowd of answerers and spectators)
the kind of question the answer is attached to (a routine homework computation versus a conceptual question that draws a crowd of expert answerers)

selected.name: Hint register and deliberate incompleteness
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the text presents itself as a partial nudge rather than a completed derivation: literal 'Hint:' labels, 'this may get you started', 'now you can solve for x', 'I'll leave the last step to you', a named theorem or trick offered without carrying it through, or a proof deliberately hidden/withheld. 0 = fully worked from premise to conclusion with nothing left to the reader; 10 = the text is nothing but a pointer or a single suggested tool. Score the extent of the hint register only. Do NOT judge whether withholding the full solution is pedagogically good or bad, and do not judge whether the hint is correct.
selected.rationale: R37 is a bare 'Hint: Apply Melanaus theorem...' one-liner; R39 is 'Hint:' plus three lines and 'Now you can solve for x'; R08 opens 'Hint:' and hides the proof in a spoiler block; R56 opens 'The following may get you started'; R55 says 'I'll leave the last step of simplifying the summation to you'. Hint register is a venue-norm habit that varies with the answerer's site experience and with the perceived homework-status of the question, and it is scorable purely from surface framing. Tagged mixed because calibrated hinting can genuinely serve the reader.
selected.upstream_parent: the answerer's practice with site homework-policy conventions (a regular who knows the norm of hinting rather than solving)
